children: Why did India's biggest public sector bank keep giving the Prashant Agarwal family another chance? A Rs 4,000-crore CDR. A Rs 934-crore debt-for-shares swap. Then a Rs 5,600-crore S4A, with Rs 2,249.74 crore declared "unsustainable" and converted into shares and debentures.
Five years later, insolvency.
Bombay Rayon's Ultimate Corporate Shell Game And SBI's Complacency

The Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) has opened an investigation into Bombay Rayon Fashions Ltd (BRFL), the Mumbai textile group that once called itself India's largest shirt manufacturer and is now in liquidation, with admitted liabilities of Rs 7,358 crore, including Rs 6,690 crore owed to financial creditors.
A summons dated August 5, 2026, reviewed by BW, states that the central government ordered SFIO to investigate BRFL's affairs on October 30, 2025, under Section 212(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013.
SFIO's director has appointed an investigating officer and two inspectors, and investigators are summoning people connected to the company for examination in New Delhi.

But sources, some of whom hold incriminating documents, believe SFIO should also thoroughly probe SBI's repeated rescue and lifeline to Bombay Rayon and its promoters, the Prashant and Janardhan Agarwal family. There is also a case of funds diversion, and the vast network of the Agarwal family's company links, "yarn supplier bills," corporate connections and subsidiary money transfers should be probed, the sources say.

The SFIO should look into assets owned by Agarwal family members and close relatives and network, and the probe should begin with officials at SBI's Mumbai branch who, the sources allege, facilitated the repeated restructurings.
The SFIO order names the company. But BRFL did not fall alone, and it did not fall quickly.
It was carried, rescue after rescue, by a consortium of public sector banks led by the State Bank of India.

How did a company go from a Rs 4,000-crore bank rescue to another Rs 2,249.74-crore debt restructuring, survive years of regulatory trouble, enter insolvency—and ultimately reach liquidation—while the same promoter family remained at the centre of the story?
SBI was not an observer.

According to restructuring documents reviewed by BW, it was the lead bank and the monitoring institution under the first restructuring, the bank responsible for watching whether the company kept its promises. In the third rescue, it took the largest share of the equity. And in August 2018, barely fifteen months after S4A, SBI put its Rs 2,260.79 crore loan exposure up for sale. JM Financial ARC ultimately acquired it for Rs 900 crore. The gap was Rs 1,361 crore, before accounting for provisions already made by SBI. That much direct loss of public money.
The rescues did not end in recovery.
They ended in insolvency. What follows is the record of what the bank could see at every step, and what it did anyway.
Red Flag One: A Profitable Company that Couldn't Pay

On paper, BRFL was still reporting a profit. In the quarter ended March 2013, net profit rose 16.6% to Rs 48.36 crore and net sales rose 12.5% to Rs 895.55 crore. Yet within weeks the company approached its lenders for restructuring.
The contradiction was stark: accounting profit on one side, a Rs 4,000-crore debt problem on the other.

After market hours on July 19, 2013, the company disclosed that its board had approved a corporate debt restructuring proposal. The stock fell nearly 8% to Rs 203.25. It had once traded as high as Rs 418, in May 2008.

A company reporting rising profits while unable to service its loans presents lenders with two possibilities: its profits weren't turning into cash, or it had borrowed far beyond what the business could carry.
Either should have triggered hard scrutiny of where the money was going. Instead, it got a rescue, with SBI as its monitor. The first restructuring was supposed to solve the debt problem. It didn't.

But there was another line buried in the company's own explanation for the crisis: "Advances to Subsidiaries." BRFL listed it alongside large-scale expansion, redemption of commercial paper, delayed government subsidies and rising debt costs as factors that had hurt its cash flows and forced it towards the Rs 4,000-crore CDR.
That raises a much bigger question than whether the company simply borrowed too much.

Why was a company heading for a Rs 4,000-crore bank rescue advancing money to subsidiaries? Which companies received it? How much? On what terms? Who controlled them? And how much of that money ever came back?
Network of Companies

The network was extensive, and it crossed borders. Company filings show BRFL held subsidiaries including Bombay Rayon Holdings Ltd, STI India Ltd, DPJ Clothing Ltd in the UK, BRFL Bangladesh Pvt Ltd, and two Italian entities, BRFL Italia S.r.l and BRFL Italia Licensee S.r.l, which held the "GURU" garment brand.
The promoter group itself included a foreign company: AAA United B.V., which held 13.83% of BRFL and is classified in the company's own filings as a foreign promoter company.

By the end, the company could not even account for several of them. Its auditors and secretarial auditors recorded that financial statements of BRFL Textiles, BRFL Italia Licensee, STI India and DPJ Clothing were simply "not available," BRFL Italia's business was closed, and BRFL Bangladesh had no operations.
A group that could not produce accounts for its own subsidiaries had been advancing them money while asking banks for thousands of crores.

The answers are buried in the related-party disclosures and the books of the subsidiaries. And that is where the trail leads away from a simple story of a textile company caught in a downturn, and towards the Agarwal family's wider corporate network.
Red Flag Two: Unpaid Interest, Rolled into Shares
By late 2015, the lenders were back.

On a Joint Lenders' Forum recommendation dated November 4, 2015, BRFL's board approved converting a Rs 712.67 crore working capital term loan and Rs 221.58 crore of funded interest term loan, Rs 934.26 crore in all, into equity for the lenders.
Interest the company couldn't pay had first been turned into a new loan.
Now that loan was turned into shares. The banks had become part-owners of a borrower that couldn't pay them.
Red Flag Three: The Workers' Money
In April 2016, the warning became impossible to miss.
The Boisar MIDC police registered a case against three BRFL directors, Prashant Agarwal, Janardhan Agarwal and Aman Agarwal.

They were accused of misappropriating Rs 1.90 crore in provident fund contributions deducted from about 1,400 workers at the company's Tarapur plant between October 2014 and December 2015. According to a Mumbai Mirror report at the time, the money was allegedly divided among the directors instead of being deposited with the government, at SBI's own Boisar branch.
The case was registered under Section 406 of the IPC for criminal breach of trust, on a complaint by a provident fund inspector.

The workers' money allegedly went missing in the very months the lenders were negotiating their second rescue; the Joint Lenders' Forum met inside that window. The case became public weeks before shareholders voted on the conversion.
By then the stock had fallen to Rs 133.60, a third below its level at the first rescue.

The accusation was not about a business misjudgment. It was about money deducted from workers' wages for their retirement. For a lender weighing whether to trust a management with thousands of crores more, it is hard to imagine a clearer signal.
And it never stopped.

Six years later, the company's own annual report disclosed that as on March 31, 2022, provident fund dues outstanding for more than six months stood at Rs 18.60 crore, employee state insurance dues at Rs 4.46 crore, and interest and penalties on PF, ESIC and TDS at Rs 15.02 crore. The Rs 1.90 crore that triggered a criminal case in 2016 had grown almost tenfold in unpaid workers' dues by 2022.
The directors stayed in charge throughout.

At the annual general meeting of September 27, 2019, shareholders reappointed Prashant Agrawal as managing director for a further two years, three years after the police case. As late as the 2021-22 annual report, Aman Agrawal and Prashant Agrawal were retiring by rotation and offering themselves for reappointment.
Red Flag Four: Losses, and a Shrinking Business
The numbers were heading the wrong way too.
In the quarter ended September 2016, BRFL reported a net loss of Rs 53.56 crore.
That was the company the lenders had in front of them when they sat down to design the next rescue.
The Third Rescue: S4A

In April 2017, a year after the PF case, the banks approved their most sweeping rescue yet, under the RBI's Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets, or S4A. It was the one of the largest debt recasts under RBI's S4A Schemes.
According to the S4A documents, the package covered about Rs 5,600 crore of debt.

Of that, Rs 2,249.74 crore was declared unsustainable and converted into equity and debentures. BRFL's board, at its meeting on April 25, 2017, approved issuing up to 126,655,304 shares on a preferential basis, representing 39.89% of the expanded share capital, plus optionally convertible debentures of face value Rs 1,000 each not exceeding Rs 410 crore, to lenders under the S4A scheme.
An extraordinary general meeting was convened on May 20, 2017 to approve it.
The Scheme Cleared a Second Gate as well.
On June 1, 2017, CNBC-TV18 reported that Bombay Rayon had obtained the banks' Oversight Committee clearance for S4A, the RBI-mandated body meant to independently vet such packages.
Who sat on that committee, what material it was shown, and what it examined are now part of the same trail. Must be investigated and it will crack the code.
SBI took the largest slice. The documents show it was allotted 43.74 million shares under S4A, plus debentures, and later another 19.31 million shares and 106,732 debentures.
For ordinary shareholders, the dilution was crushing.

By January 2018, BRFL's equity capital stood at Rs 317.48 crore against Rs 134.60 crore in 2013. The share count had more than doubled, and the new shares went mostly to lenders swapping bad loans, not to investors bringing fresh money. The end result: by March 2022, financial institutions and banks held 51.88% of Bombay Rayon Fashions.
The lenders owned the company.

S4A was meant for stressed borrowers whose businesses were considered capable of servicing at least half their debt. In BRFL's case, lenders classified Rs 3,390 crore, about 60% of the Rs 5,600-crore package, as sustainable.

So what does it imply? One of three things, and each is a story: the projections behind the classification assumed a recovery that hadn't happened and had no basis in the company's results; the projections rested on figures supplied by a management already facing a criminal complaint, and nobody independently verified them; or the number was worked backwards from the answer the lenders needed, which was a sustainable share above 50%.
They applied that test to a company that had failed a CDR, needed a debt-for-shares swap, was reporting quarterly losses, and whose directors faced a criminal complaint over workers' money.
The company's own results soon showed what those cash flows really were. In the quarter ended September 2017, BRFL lost Rs 14.56 crore, and its net sales fell 31.2% to Rs 675.05 crore.
The Share Price Spike and The Crash
Then the stock went on a ride no fundamentals could explain.
From a low of Rs 111 on October 17, 2017, BRFL's shares nearly doubled in two months, reaching Rs 232.50 on December 18.
The business hadn't turned around; it was still losing money and shrinking.
Then the floor gave way. From a close of Rs 224.75 on December 15, 2017, the stock fell 49.96% in eleven trading sessions to Rs 112.45, locked at the lower circuit on January 2, 2018.
The rally came months after the S4A price had been set, so it did not affect the conversion.

But a loss-making company's stock doubling and halving within weeks, just after India's largest bank became one of its biggest shareholders, raises questions SEBI's trading records can answer: who bought on the way up, and who sold on the way down?
The Exit That Wasn't
By mid-2018, SBI owned 29.28% of BRFL, more than any other institution; Axis Bank held 8.04%, and six other lenders between 1.61% and 3.35% each.

In August 2018, barely fifteen months after approving S4A, SBI put the account up for sale to asset reconstruction companies, banks and NBFCs, showing dues of Rs 2,260.79 crore, not counting its equity. JM Financial ARC bought the loan.
According to an analysis by Capitalmind, it paid Rs 900 crore for SBI's Rs 2,261 crore exposure, a haircut of about 60%, with Rs 840 crore in cash and the rest in security receipts.
In May 2017, lenders had certified Rs 3,390 crore of this company's debt as sustainable.
Fifteen months later, SBI was selling at 40 paise on the rupee.
But the bank never got out.

Long after selling the loan, SBI remained BRFL's single largest shareholder: the company's 2021-22 annual report shows State Bank of India holding 91,352,087 shares, or 28.77%, on March 31, 2022, with Axis Bank holding 25,520,484 shares or 8.04%. Those shares were, by then, worth a fraction of the debt they had replaced.
Other lenders scrambled out. Punjab National Bank sold its entire holding of about 7.58 million shares in a series of trades between October 2021 and February 2022, ending with zero.

Promoter shares were being sold too: Ashwell Holding Company Pvt Ltd, a promoter entity, ran its stake down from 7.92% to 1.39% during 2021-22, and Prashant Agrawal's own holding fell after what the company described as invocation of pledge by the lender.
The Rs 888 Crore that Vanished into Write-offs
Then came the accounting reckoning, and it points straight at the sources' allegations about supplier bills and money moving out of the company.
In 2021-22, BRFL's loss ballooned from Rs 299.95 crore to Rs 1,147.20 crore.

The company's explanation, in its own directors' report: the loss was "mainly because of writing off of loss incurred by the company in value of obsolete & non-moving inventory and writing off of non-recoverable debts." The extraordinary item alone came to Rs 888.07 crore.
Nearly Rs 900 crore of inventory and receivables written off in a single year.

Who owed those non-recoverable debts? What inventory became worthless, and when was it bought? These are precisely the questions the SFIO's and CBI inspectors can put to the company's auditors, and precisely the ledgers the sources say should be examined alongside the yarn supplier bills.
Two facts sit alongside that write-off.
First, the directors' report for the same year states that there were no instances of fraud reported by the statutory auditors under Section 143(12) of the Companies Act.
Second, in that same year of a Rs 1,147 crore loss and Rs 18.60 crore of unpaid provident fund dues, chairman and managing director Aman Agrawal drew Rs 2.35 crore in salary and allowances.
The Asset that Moved Out
While the parent company sank, its best business was moved into a new vehicle.

BRFL Textiles Private Limited was incorporated on August 20, 2020, and shareholders approved the transfer of the Tarapur undertaking by way of a slump sale as a going concern to BRFL Textiles at the annual general meeting of September 30, 2020.
The effect is visible in the numbers.

In 2021-22, BRFL itself generated revenue of just Rs 83.08 crore, because "the major business of manufacturing of finished fabrics was demerged by the Company during the FY 2020-21." The new company, in which BRFL held 70%, reported turnover of Rs 731.67 crore, total assets of Rs 1,101.61 crore and a loss of Rs 218.36 crore on provisional figures, though even those were unaudited, because its financials were not available to its own parent.
Nine times the revenue of the listed company it came out of, sitting in an entity whose accounts the listed parent could not obtain, in the two years before that parent was admitted into insolvency.
The Collapse
The company later conceded that the rescues had failed.
In a 2020 statement, it said its debts had been restructured twice under RBI schemes, but that they never supplied the working capital it needed, so its factories were never fully used.
By September 2020, BRFL owed about Rs 51.1 billion, and its revenue had fallen 61% in a year to Rs 2.5 billion, with a loss before interest and tax.
Its own annual return shows total indebtedness of Rs 4,704.74 crore as on April 1, 2021, of which Rs 4,692.29 crore was interest due but not paid.

In August 2021, managing director Prashant Agarwal was arrested by the Mumbai unit of the Directorate General of GST Intelligence in an alleged Rs 55.8 crore input tax credit fraud; he was booked under the CGST Act and remanded to judicial custody.

By May 2022 the company had stopped being a functioning listed entity at all: the stock exchanges suspended trading in its securities from May 23, 2022, for non-compliance with SEBI's listing regulations and non-payment of fines and listing fees.
The end came from a yarn trader owed Rs 1.61 crore.

On June 7, 2022, the NCLT admitted BRFL into insolvency on the petition of Vikash Parasprampuria, sole proprietor of Chiranjilal Yarn Traders. Prashant Agrawal's appeal against admission was dismissed by the NCLAT on July 15, 2022. JM Financial's admitted claim of Rs 6,080 crore gave it 90.80% of the votes on the committee of creditors, with Axis Bank's admitted claim of Rs 610.86 crore making up the rest. Though Donear, Welspun and Arvind had shown interest, the creditors rejected every plan, and on November 9, 2023, the tribunal ordered liquidation.
The stock that once traded at Rs 418 hit an all-time low of Rs 1.58 on December 5, 2022, when the whole company was worth about Rs 58 crore.
Why SFIO and CBI Must look Inside the Bank

Line the warning signs up: A restructuring requested on the back of rising profits; money advanced to subsidiaries whose accounts the parent could not obtain; interest capitalised and swapped for shares; a criminal complaint alleging directors took workers' retirement money; quarterly losses; a share price in free fall.
Every one was visible before SBI and its partners approved S4A. The bank did not need hindsight. It needed only to read its own files.
So why did SBI keep saying yes?

Perhaps the bankers believed, against the evidence, that one more rescue would work. Perhaps a bad loan restructured is a bad loan not yet recognised, and deferring the loss suited someone's balance sheet or career.

Or perhaps there was something else. Whether this was a failure of judgment, a failure of diligence, or something worse is precisely what an investigation must establish, and precisely what no one has yet been asked to explain.

SFIO investigates companies, and its order names BRFL. But the Companies Act gives its inspectors wide powers to examine records and people connected to a company's affairs, and no records are more connected to BRFL's affairs than its lead bank's loan files: the internal sanction notes for each rescue, the Joint Lenders' Forum minutes, the CDR Empowered Group papers, the S4A viability assessment and techno-economic viability report, the papers placed before the RBI-mandated Oversight Committee, the cash-flow projections behind the "sustainable" debt figure, and the promoter contributions the banks demanded or failed to demand.
If those files point to lapses inside the banks, the CBI, the RBI and SBI's own vigilance wing will need to follow.
The questions are simple, and they deserve answers under oath
Who at SBI recommended and approved each rescue?
Did they read the 2016 police complaint before approving S4A, and if so, why did they leave the same directors in charge?
What cash-flow figures made a loss-making, shrinking company "60% sustainable," and what was placed before the Oversight Committee?
Did any lender examine the advances to subsidiaries, or the Rs 888.07 crore of inventory and receivables written off in a single year?
Did anyone examine the 2017 rally and crash in a stock the bank had just become a major owner of?
And after losing more than Rs 1,300 crore on one account, while still holding 28.77% of a company worth Rs 58 crore, did India's largest bank ask a single official to explain?
BW sent detailed questions to SBI but has received no reply.
A response will be incorporated as and when SBI chooses to provide one.

BW Reporters Palak Shah is a seasoned investigative journalist and the fearless author of The Market Mafia: Chronicle of India’s High-Tech Stock Market Scandal & The Cabal That Went Scot-Free, a hard-hitting exposé that unmasked the shadowy underbelly of India’s financial markets.

With nearly two decades of boots-on-the-ground reporting in Mumbai, Palak has carved a reputation as a relentless truth-seeker, diving deep into the nexus of money, power, and regulation. His bylines have graced India’s most prestigious financial dailies, including The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Financial Express, and The Hindu Business Line, where his incisive coverage has shaped narratives and rattled boardrooms.

Drawn to crime reporting at the tender age of 19, Palak quickly realized that Mumbai’s gritty gang wars of the 1980s had given way to a slicker, more insidious form of organized crime—white-collar schemes orchestrated in corporate towers. This epiphany fueled his pivot to financial journalism, where he’s spent years decoding the complex machinations of India’s ‘white money’ economy.

From stock market manipulations to regulatory loopholes, Palak’s work peels back the polished veneer of high finance to reveal the cabals pulling the strings. His passion for uncovering truth, backed by a knack for connecting dots others miss, makes him a formidable voice in Indian journalism, unafraid to challenge the status quo and expose the players who think they’re untouchable.
